web.title: Why Y Combinator is backing fewer African startups
web.description:
- [Home](https://disruptafrica.com/)
  - [Startups](https://disruptafrica.com/category/startups/)

Lagos founders talked about the accelerator as a rite of passage, and the [Paystack exit to Stripe](https://disruptafrica.com/2020/10/15/nigerian-fintech-startup-paystack-acquired-by-stripe-in-landmark-moment-for-african-tech-ecosystem/) made the path look repeatable.

The accelerator went fully remote from Summer 2020, ballooned its batches, and African founders who could never have relocated to San Francisco for three months suddenly could apply from Lagos or Nairobi.

For a founder in Accra or Kigali, that means a US visa, a quarter away from customers and staff, and San Francisco rents paid from a pre-seed budget. The remote years removed those costs; the return to campus put them back.

When it recovered in 2025, to [US$1.6 billion over the course of the year](https://disruptafrica.gumroad.com/l/kjrnr) – note, [2026 is likely to be similar to this](https://disruptafrica.com/2026/10/05/58-african-tech-startups-raise-583m-in-funding-in-q3/) – the money went mostly to large rounds.

Iyin Aboyeji’s Future Africa launched Accelerate Africa, openly pitched as a home-grown answer to YC.

The broader accelerator map is shrinking, though.

web.title: Grants aren't a consolation prize: rethinking non-dilutive ...
web.description:
- [Home](https://disruptafrica.com/)
  - [Startups](https://disruptafrica.com/category/startups/)

[Search](https://disruptafrica.com/2026/11/10/grants-arent-a-consolation-prize-rethinking-non-dilutive-capital-for-early-stage-founders/#)

Founders have filled that gap with whatever capital doesn’t ask for equity: national innovation agency grants, foundation-backed programmes, fellowships with stipends, prize money from pitch competitions, hyper-scaler cloud credits, and – increasingly – [grants and small cheques from blockchain ecosystem funds looking for builders in emerging markets](https://disruptafrica.com/2026/01/19/hashgraph-ventures-pledges-1m-to-hedera-africa-hackathon-to-accelerate-web3-ai-innovation/).

A founder who gives up 10 to 15 per cent of the company in a pre-seed round to buy 12 months of runway has paid for that time with the most expensive currency they own. A founder who buys the same 12 months with three grants and a credits package has paid in paperwork.

Grant money gives founders room to do the slow, unglamorous work – regulatory approvals, pilots with public health systems, agri-tech field trials – that many African businesses need before they can scale at all.

A startup that walks into a seed conversation with US$150,000 in non-dilutive funding, a pilot and a clean cap table is negotiating from strength, not asking for rescue.
